newsitem.title: USA: Peres election move stymied Syria deal - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Peres election move stymied Syria deal - envoy.

text.p: A decision by former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres to call early elections last year torpedoed chances of an Israel-Syria peace agreement, Syria's ambassador to Washington said in a newly published interview.

The envoy, Walid al-Moualem, told the Journal of Palestine Studies that Peres' move made an accord impossible after the two sides had agreed on a June 1996 deadline for nailing down the elements of a deal.

Peres and his Labour Party, then riding high in Israeli opinion polls, decided about a year ago to advance elections from October to May of last year, confident of a new mandate to pursue peace with the Arabs.

But Palestinian suicide bombings in Israel in February and March created a more hawkish mood there. Peres eventually lost the elections to right-wing Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu, who has taken a much tougher line on peace with Syria.
Moualem, who played a key role in Israel-Syria peace talks until they were suspended by Israel last February in reaction to the suicide bombings, described Peres' move as an error.
"Once elections are scheduled, you can't reach an agreement when you are not sure about the results," he told the Washington-based magazine.
Moualem said that following progress in the talks, Israel, Syria and U.S. mediators had agreed last January to hold continuous talks to reach an outline agreement.

"We set a deadline for ourselves, agreeing to close the remaining gaps and finalise all the elements of an agreement by June of 1996, at which time we would send what we had agreed to a special drafting committee," he said.
"The expectation was that by September 1996 the final document would be ready."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns declined to comment directly on the interview. He told a news briefing: "If there had been an Israel-Syria agreement ... in 1995, we wouldn't be standing here debating this."
Privately, however, U.S. officials have said that Syria's President Hafez al-Assad had backed away from a peace deal with Israel even before the elections were advanced.

Moualem repeated assertions by Assad that the former Labour government promised Syria it would withdraw from the occupied Golan Heights -- the main point of contention in the peace talks -- to the demarcation lines of June 4, 1967.
Other reports have said Labour agreed to a slightly less extensive withdrawal in the event of a peace deal.

Israel's ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben Elissar, said on Wednesday: "There is no agreement of any kind between Israel and the United States or between Israel, the United States and Syria that entails Israel's acceptance to withdraw from the Golan Heights to the line of 1967."

The United States has been trying to revive the Israeli-Syrian talks, which originally began in 1991, but Syria has shown little interest because of Likud's declared policy of holding on to the Golan.

An Israeli newspaper and security sources said on Wednesday, however, that Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai had ordered the army to examine the country's security needs should Israel return parts of the Golan Heights to Syria in a peace deal.
